titleStmt.title: Topic modeling in the digital humanities: On replicability and transparency

dhq:bio.p: Diego Emanuel Giménez Celano is a professor of Portuguese Literature at the University of Macau. He was a fellow of the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation and a researcher in the project No Problem Has a Solution: A Digital Archive of the Book of Disquiet at the University of Coimbra. He was a postdoctoral researcher at the State University of Londrina, is a member of Camões Lab, and is the principal investigator of the University of Macau project Portuguese Literary Studies: Texts, Readings, and Digital Approaches.

dhq:authorInfo.dhq:affiliation: WU Vienna University of Economics and Business

dhq:bio.p: Mathew Gillings is an Assistant Professor at the WU Vienna University of Economics and Business. His research applies corpus methods to topics in (critical) discourse analysis, forensic linguistics, and (im)politeness. He is Associate Editor of Pragmatics, the author of Corpus Linguistic Approaches to Deception Detection (Routledge, 2024), and a co-author of Corpus-Assisted Discourse Studies (CUP, 2023).

dhq:abstract.p: Topic models are highly sensitive to corpus construction, preprocessing, stopword removal, segmentation, model implementation, and the selected number of topics. Yet rather than present these limitations as something new, this article revisits topic modeling to ask what standards of transparency and reproducibility should follow from them. Through a case study of Fernando Pessoa’s Livro do Desassossego (The Book of Disquiet), we compare topic modeling outputs across different editorial versions, preprocessing conditions, and modeling configurations. Using Quanteda for corpus preparation and document–feature matrix construction, and seededlda for unsupervised and guided topic modeling, we show how apparently technical decisions shape outcomes. The article argues that topic modeling should be understood as an exploratory interpretive procedure rather than as a neutral mechanism for discovering themes. Its scholarly value depends on making the full modeling pipeline — from source acquisition and cleaning to parameter selection, code, derived data, and interpretation — available for inspection, reuse, and critical contestation.

div.head: 1. Introduction
div.p: Topic modeling (TM) is a method with roots in computer science and text mining, but has since been applied to, and used within, the digital humanities. Topic modeling is a method that should sound appealing to most scholars working with textual data within the humanities and social sciences: It allows the user to input a large corpus of texts, and it then algorithmically detects patterns of meaning for the researcher to interpret and explore further. It appears to take the subjectivity of the researcher out of the equation and returns a set of mathematically derived topics for probing. According to David M. Blei, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) is claimed to be the simplest of TM approaches . It is suggested that LDA can discover the hidden thematic structure of a collection of texts and that topic models can be used to explore, visualise, and summarise a corpus .

But these are bold claims which invite critical introspection, both at the level of the algorithm and the interpretation by the researcher. After all, scholars working in neighbouring research communities, such as corpus linguistics, know all too well how important it is to interpret quantitative results within the wider textual (and indeed social) context, rather than simply presenting a mathematical output . In Section 2, we will offer an introduction to TM and how it is used to analyse discourse. In Section 3, we will consider the use of topic modeling in literature, specifically in its use to interrogate literary texts. We will briefly explore a method to topic model a literary corpus using Quanteda, an R package used to build and process corpora. In particular, we opted to use Quanteda for corpus management, tokenization, preprocessing, and document-feature matrix construction, and seededlda for the topic modeling stage. This distinction matters because our argument concerns the sequence of decisions through which textual materials are transformed into model inputs. Quanteda is therefore used here primarily to make preprocessing inspectable and reproducible, while seededlda provides the LDA and seeded LDA implementations used in the analysis. Quanteda, more than a topic modeling engine in this paper, ensures that model inputs are constructed in a consistent, inspectable, and reproducible way. This workflow provides an end-to-end, scriptable pipeline in which preprocessing decisions are explicitly documented. In comparing the outcomes, we highlight how differences in both data preparation and code have a direct impact on the outcome of the analysis. In Section 4 we move on to a more critical discussion of issues with the method and interpretation, and in Section 5 we conclude with a summary and final discussion of best practices.

Since the adoption of topic modeling in digital humanities during the 2010s, scholars have repeatedly noted that topic models are sensitive to preprocessing choices, stopword lists, the selected number of topics, random initialization, corpus construction, and the interpretation of ranked word lists. Early work in macroanalysis and literary topic modeling showed how probabilistic models could support large-scale exploration of textual collections and offer new ways to identify patterns not immediately visible through close reading alone . At the same time, DH scholars and critics have raised substantial concerns about the interpretability, stability, and evidentiary status of topic models . These concerns include the selection of K, the treatment of stopwords, the instability of probabilistic models across runs, the tendency to equate ranked word lists with meaningful themes, and the risk of treating computational outputs as if they were transparent representations of textual meaning. This article accepts these critiques as the starting point rather than as objections to be dismissed. Instead, our purpose here is to show how topic modeling can be framed as an exploratory and reproducible interpretive procedure, provided that its assumptions and transformations are explicitly documented.

The emphasis on transparency also connects our argument to recent discussions of reproducibility and repetitive research in digital humanities. Christof Schöch argues that digital humanities need a more precise vocabulary for practices such as replication, reproduction, reanalysis, reinvestigation, revision, and reuse, because computational humanities research is rarely repeated under perfectly identical conditions . This is relevant for topic modeling, where any changes may constitute a reanalysis or reinvestigation of the same textual materials. Our argument therefore treats replicability as the creation of sufficiently documented conditions under which a topic modeling workflow can be inspected, rerun, modified, and critically evaluated. Only under such conditions can we determine whether any differences in results — if they appear — stem from the text, from methodological choices, or from assumptions inherent within the modeling process.

div.head: 2. Topic modeling
div.p: Let us begin with a brief overview of topic modeling. Topic modeling is a machine learning algorithm that traces word co-occurrence within individual texts across a corpus. After running the algorithm, two outputs are presented to the researcher: The first is a list of topics (represented by a list of co-occurring words that are strongly linked to each topic); and the second is a composition document, which shows the distribution of those topics across texts. Upon receiving the list of words, researchers may optionally assign labels to them to facilitate discussion. This may consist of inspecting top terms, close reading texts with high topic proportions, and/or triangulating with other methods. These labels do not technically constitute the topic itself; they are a convenient summary of a probabilistic distribution and should be treated as interpretive and provisional. Yet in carrying out the act of labelling, the analyst also carries out an act of interpretation — because ultimately, the label goes some way towards reifying the topic. Care must be taken here not to conflate the technical meaning of topic (i.e., as the probabilistic distribution of words) with the qualitative interpretation (i.e., after labelling has taken place).
In all, topic modeling makes four main assumptions (adapted from and ):

list.item: The overall corpus consists of a large number of documents;
Each document features each of the topics to varying degrees; and finally
Underlying topics organise the corpus, and there are a finite number of these topics

div.p: Indeed, also makes the important point that one cannot equate topics (in the statistical sense) to themes or categories — an interpretive leap that some researchers fall into the trap of making.

present an overview of how a topic modeling algorithm works below the surface, using a bucket metaphor: This assumption, that documents are created by random word selection without concern for order, grammar, or discourse structure, can be visualized concretely via buckets. Let us imagine that each topic is a bucket. Within the buckets are small cards with words written on them. Every word appears in every bucket at least once. But each bucket contains many duplicates of some words. An author sits amidst the buckets and builds a text by pulling cards from the buckets. At the outset, they decide which buckets to draw from, and what fraction of the text will be drawn from each. Word by word, the author pulls a random card from a bucket, and copies its word down before returning it to the bucket, until the document reaches its pre-decided length. Words strongly linked to a particular topic emerge more often in documents that draw on that topic more heavily, because cards marked with those words are more common in that topic’s bucket .

Before running the algorithm, the researcher has control over various parameters: the number of topics that should be found; the inclusion or exclusion of stopwords; the number of sampling iterations; and model-estimation settings. Depending on the implementation used, additional parameters such as number of iterations or a random seed may also be appropriate to consider. Depending on the implementation, the researcher may also evaluate alternative hyperparameter settings (e.g., document-topic and topic-word concentration parameters) by comparing model quality across runs. Each of these parameters deserves critical attention, not least because it is the decisions made here at the outset that influence the type of result one will receive on the other side. After all, as Monika Bednarek states, TM is a technique where initial decisions affect subsequent results, and researchers need to be suitably informed of the effects of these decisions .

With regard to the first parameter, predetermining the number of topics that should be found by the algorithm may appear, to many researchers, slightly counterintuitive. After all, interpretation follows the data in traditional discourse-analytic work, and something as subjective as a topic is largely seen as something for the researcher to determine, rather than an algorithm. The number of topics that could (or should) be in a corpus differs depending on a wide range of factors, and much interpretive work relies on those topics coming organically from the data, suited to individual research questions and aims (some work is top-down and led by theory, of course, but even these forms would never stipulate a target number). However, the algorithm needs at least some prior information to run, and this is therefore a necessary stipulation. Unfortunately, there is little guidance on how to determine an optimal number of topics. Derek Greene et al. suggest that setting too few topics may lead to overly broad results, whereas too many may result in an over-clustering where it is difficult to determine exactly what the topic means (and, thus, make topic labelling difficult) . Published works making use of topic modeling vary in the number of topics requested; suggest that trial and error is the best way to determine what works for each individual study, whereas went a step further and developed a classification task, systematically varying the number of topics (and other parameters), to help determine the optimal number for their particular dataset and research objective. Ultimately, it is a subjective decision that may be defended on the grounds of usefulness but not on the grounds of accuracy .

Similarly, deciding whether to remove stopwords is another largely subjective decision. A stoplist generally consists of function words (such as determiners, pronouns, prepositions, etc.), and as with most work within Natural Language Processing (NLP), topic modeling suites offer the option of automatically removing them from the analysis. Quanteda has a stopwords library to impose a default stoplist. Of course, within the context of Mike Scott’s finding that grammatical keywords indicate style and content keywords indicate aboutness , this is something that may make corpus linguists wince. Removing grammatical words from the outset, before they have even had the chance to prove themselves as interesting, seems to go against the very nature of such work, which instead favours this process of discovery. There also appears to be empirical support for that position: In assessing model quality across three configurations, Alexandra Schofield et al. find that it does not make much difference whether stopwords are removed before or after modeling, but doing so later has benefits in terms of improving efficiency and removing epistemological bias .

Subjectivity in methodological decision-making is not a problem in and of itself. All empirical research methods involve some degree of subjectivity, whether it is during data collection, processing, analysis, or interpretation. Thus, deciding on the optimal number of topics, and deciding whether to remove stopwords, are both ultimately decisions that only the human analyst can make. It is due to this that Akira Murakami et al. suggest that these decisions can also be seen as a strength, and being forced into making two relatively arbitrary decisions at the outset means that the analytical subjectivity cannot be masked . As analysts, then, we are tasked with understanding the quantitative implications of our qualitative decision-making.

div.head: 3. Topic modeling applied to literary texts
div.p: In this section, we examine a TM method applied to The Book of Disquiet by Fernando Pessoa using Quanteda (accessed via R). Fernando Pessoa, a Portuguese modernist writer, authored over 700 texts for The Book of Disquiet between 1913 and 1935. However, he passed away before completing the book, leaving it unfinished. Since then, scholars have edited The Book of Disquiet in various ways, interpreting the fragmented material Pessoa left behind. The book has four major editions (1982, 1990, 1998, 2010), each differing in fragment selection, ordering, readings, and heteronym attribution — all reflecting diverse perspectives on this fragmented and unfinished work. Additionally, Pessoa’s use of an old Portuguese orthography has resulted in differences in the linguistic choices across editions.

Drawing upon the work of , who developed an R guide applied to Pessoa’s book, here we aim to demonstrate the impact of three decisions that researchers must make in the process of preparing a corpus for a topic modeling analysis: (1) the version of the text (i.e., the old or modern version); (2) the extent to which a corpus is edited and which stopwords are removed (i.e., raw vs. cleaned data); and (3) the specific topic modeling algorithm being utilised to perform the analysis.

In Section 3.1, we systematically examine the influence of: (1) edition/orthography; and (2) preprocessing decisions. Our workflow uses Quanteda for corpus management and transparent preprocessing, and seededlda for topic modeling. We analyze four corpus conditions defined by two dimensions. The first dimension is the edition under analysis — (a) the 1982 edition in historical Portuguese; and (b) the 1998 edition in modernized Portuguese. The second dimension is whether the corpus is analyzed in a raw form or a cleaned form. Here, cleaning refers to: (a) removing extraneous paratextual materials (e.g., editors’ introductions and edition-related metadata, where present); and (b) removing stopwords. Stopwords were defined using a default Portuguese stopword list The stopwords package for R provides a centralised resource for stopword lists across multiple languages and sources. It aims to eliminate the need for text analysis or NLP packages to incorporate their own stopword lists or functions. https://stopwords.quanteda.io/., supplemented with additional items deemed relevant for this study When working with corpora featuring older forms of Portuguese, such as texts employing archaic grammar and orthography, it is often necessary to manually edit the default stopword list provided by the package. Words like elle (modern ele) and aquelle (modern aquele), among others, were manually added to ensure effective filtering. Constructing a tailored list of stopwords adapted to historical language forms greatly improves the quality of text analysis in research involving older corpora., and all modifications are documented in the accompanying code. Because preprocessing choices can substantially affect topic model outputs, as mentioned above — especially in non-English corpora — we make these steps explicit and report them to minimize avoidable bias and facilitate replication.

The corpus was prepared from edition-level PDF files of the 1982 and 1998 editions of Livro do Desassossego. The texts were extracted through OCR and then processed in R. The workflow documented in the accompanying R Markdown file specifies the input files, tokenization procedures, punctuation/number/symbol removal, stopword lists, document–feature matrix construction, and topic modeling functions. No lemmatization was applied. This decision was deliberate: Because the comparison involves historical and modernized Portuguese, lemmatization would introduce an additional layer of linguistic normalization that could obscure precisely the orthographic variation under examination.

In the original analysis, each edition-level file was treated as a single document. This decision preserves the integrity of each edition as a corpus condition, but it also has methodological consequences. Topic models are sensitive to the definition of the document unit, and long or internally heterogeneous documents may produce topics that combine several local lexical patterns. In response to this limitation, we added a supplementary segmentation robustness check. The preprocessed token streams were divided into fixed-length chunks of approximately 500 tokens, while preserving metadata linking each chunk to its source edition, preprocessing condition, and position in the original token sequence. The same preprocessing decisions, stopword lists, number of topics, and modeling package were then used to rerun the LDA models on the chunked corpus. This supplementary analysis is not intended to replace the document-level model, but to test whether the principal lexical patterns remain visible when the document unit is changed.

In Section 3.2, we analyse two additional conditions — this time related to the specific TM algorithm used. All other variables remain constant, so we use a cleaned version (i.e., with extraneous content and stopwords removed) of The Book of Disquiet written in modern Portuguese. We use two modeling configurations within the seededlda framework. First, we estimate a baseline unsupervised LDA model (textmodel_lda()), in which topics are inferred solely from word co-occurrence patterns in the data. Second, we estimate a seeded (guided) LDA model (textmodel_seededlda()), which incorporates a researcher-defined dictionary of seed words to encourage the model to form topics around predefined concepts. In this sense, seeded LDA is best understood as a semi-supervised (or guided) approach: The model remains probabilistic and data-driven, but the seed dictionary provides structured prior information that can improve interpretability and support hypothesis-driven comparisons. In comparing these two conditions, we thus ask: Are there differences between the outcomes of the analysis? Does how the corpus is prepared affect the results? Can both corpus handling (e.g., stopwords) and the code used significantly impact the results and their representations? How can one choose between tools? To answer these questions, in each condition we set the model to estimate 10 topics and then reported the top 10 terms for each topic as a concise summary of the topic–word distributions. Note that in LDA, a topic is a probability distribution over the full vocabulary; listing the top terms is a reporting convention rather than a definition of the topic.

div.head: 3.1. Examining the effect of corpus version and cleaning
div.p: Since Pessoa wrote in a form of Portuguese that predates the 1911 linguistic reform, editors have published his work in various historical variants of the language. When studying such corpora with the aid of algorithms, it is crucial to account for potential biases that may enter from outside the analysis. Quantitative methods like TM can introduce biases stemming from the linguistic assumptions embedded in their algorithms. These tools are often developed based on contemporary language structures, which may not adequately capture the nuances of texts written in pre-1911 Portuguese. With this in mind, a key question emerged during the preparation of this paper: Would there be differences in the TM outcomes when applied to each version of the corpus?

In Table 1, LdoD stands for Livro do Desassossego (Book of Disquiet). LdoD3 and LdoD4 represent corpora derived from the first edition edited by Jacinto do Prado Coelho (1982), with token counts of 165,013 (LdoD3) and 158,115 (LdoD4). LdoD3 includes Pessoa’s text together with paratextual material (the editor’s introduction and edition-related metadata), whereas LdoD4 contains only Pessoa’s text. LdoD1 and LdoD2 correspond to Richard Zenith’s 1998 edition, with token counts of 205,686 (raw) and 178,043 (cleaned). Importantly, Zenith’s edition incorporates additional fragments discovered in Pessoa’s archive at the Biblioteca Nacional de Portugal, which contributes to the higher token counts in the 1998 corpora.

Topic models require selecting the number of topics (K), and the right value depends on both the size and internal heterogeneity of the corpus as well as the desired level of interpretive granularity. Because the Livro do Desassossego is a single-work corpus (158k–206k tokens across conditions), we aimed for a parsimonious model that yields interpretable, high-level patterns rather than fine-grained subtopics. We therefore report results for K=10 as a compromise between underfitting (too few topics collapsing distinct lexical regimes) and overfitting (too many topics producing fragmented or unstable clusters).

Compared to many topic modeling applications that aggregate many documents across large corpora, a single-book corpus of 200k tokens is relatively small. This has two implications: Topic solutions may be more sensitive to preprocessing choices and the value of K, and topics should not be treated as stable themes in a strong sense but as exploratory, model-based summaries of lexical co-occurrence patterns in this specific text collection. In a single-work setting, our goal is not exhaustive thematic discovery but a reproducible way to surface how the data handling affects the outcome of the analysis.

As noted above, these corpora therefore vary along two distinct dimensions: (1) orthography (historical vs modernized Portuguese); and (2) corpus composition (differences in editorial selection and the inclusion of additional fragments and/or paratext). As a result, between-edition differences observed in topic models cannot be attributed to orthography alone; they may also reflect differences in the underlying textual materials. We therefore treat the four conditions below as a structured set of analyses that primarily supports within-edition comparisons of preprocessing choices (raw vs. cleaned), while between-edition comparisons are interpreted as reflecting a combination of orthographic modernization and editorial composition. Based on these distinctions, initial topic modeling analyses were conducted under four conditions:

list.item: Condition 1: seededlda::textmodel_lda algorithm applied to a raw old Portuguese corpus (1982 edition), without stopword removal.
Condition 2: seededlda::textmodel_lda algorithm applied to a cleaned old Portuguese corpus (1982 edition), with stopword removal.
Condition 3: seededlda::textmodel_lda algorithm applied to a raw modern Portuguese corpus (1998 edition), without stopword removal.
Condition 4: seededlda::textmodel_lda algorithm applied to a cleaned modern Portuguese corpus (1998 edition), with stopword removal.

div.head: Condition 1
div.p: In Condition 1, the unsupervised LDA topic model algorithm was applied to a raw old Portuguese corpus (1982 edition), without stopword removal.

figure.figDesc: The ten highest-probability terms for each of ten topics in the raw 1982 corpus, with Topic 6 dominated by high-frequency function words that were not removed during preprocessing.

figure.figDesc: Hierarchical clustering of the topics from the raw 1982 corpus, showing Topic 6 as an outlier because of its concentration of high-frequency function words.

div.p: In Figure 1, TM is conducted using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA): The output displays the top 10 terms for each topic, representing the terms most strongly associated with each topic in the LDA model. Some stopwords from old Portuguese orthography are evident, such as d’um (of a) and nellas (in them). Topic 6 highlights the presence of common words like que (that), de (of), and a (the), among others – to be expected, given that stopwords were not removed in this raw version of the corpus.

The prominence of high-frequency grammatical words is also reflected in the exploratory hierarchical clustering shown in Figure 2, which groups topics by similarity in their topic-word distributions. In this visualization, topics that appear closer in the dendrogram have more similar lexical-probabilistic profiles (given the chosen representation and distance metric), whereas larger branch heights indicate greater dissimilarity.

In Figure 2, the clustering suggests a coarse separation between two groups of topics. One group (Topics 1, 3, 5, 7, and 8) is characterized by high-probability terms associated with loss, memory, identity, and affect; another group (Topics 2, 4, 9, and 10) foregrounds terms linked to reflection, individuality, and abstraction. We treat this partition as a heuristic summary of topic similarity rather than as a definitive thematic taxonomy. Topic 6, dominated by function words, appears as an outlier, consistent with a stopword topic that captures weakly informative high-frequency terms; we therefore interpret it as an artifact of preprocessing and report sensitivity checks with this topic excluded.

div.head: Condition 2
div.p: In Condition 2, the unsupervised LDA topic model algorithm was applied to a cleaned old Portuguese corpus (1982 edition), with stopword removal.

figure.head: TM applying the LDA topic model package to the cleaned corpus of the 1982 edition with old Portuguese orthography.
figure.figDesc: The ten highest-probability terms for each of ten topics in the cleaned 1982 corpus, where stopword removal produces more readily interpretable lexical groupings.

figure.head: Hierarchical clustering of the TM results from analyzing the cleaned corpus of the 1982 edition with old Portuguese orthography.
figure.figDesc: Hierarchical clustering of the topics from the cleaned 1982 corpus, with Topic 5 separated from two broader groups of lexically similar topics.

div.p: The figures above illustrate notable differences from those in Condition 1, thus suggesting a noticeable impact of the decision to clean the corpus. Figure 3 presents the TM applied to a cleaned corpus based on the 1982 edition, which uses old Portuguese orthography. In this case, stopwords were removed along with certain unwanted tokens that the algorithm could not process due to the limitations of the predefined stopwords list. The outcome differs from that shown in Figure 1: The LdoD4 model — with improved preprocessing — produces a cleaner thematic structure. Topic 5 appears isolated showing some thematic macrostructure common to the whole work, composed of existential terms, representing the philosophical heart of the work. Among the remaining topics, the dendrogram indicates two main clusters. On the left, Topics 1, 2, 3, and 7 form a compact grouping, suggesting comparatively high lexical overlap among their topic-word distributions. On the right, two smaller groupings are visible — Topics 6 and 8, and Topics 4 and 10 — with Topic 9 attaching to the (6, 8) group before the right-side topics merge. These groupings should be read as exploratory signals of similarity (given the chosen representation and distance metric), and they invite interpretive follow-up (e.g., reading high-loading passages, checking topic prevalence across fragments, and assessing whether Topic 5 behaves like a background topic via dispersion and exclusivity diagnostics).

Differences between earlier figures and Figure 4 are expected, since removing stopwords (especially modern/archaic and context-specific lists) changes the effective vocabulary and can substantially alter the learned topic–word distributions. We therefore interpret changes in the clustering pattern primarily as preprocessing-driven shifts in the model input space, not as definitive evidence of a changed thematic structure.

div.head: Condition 3
div.p: In Condition 3, the unsupervised LDA topic model algorithm was applied to a raw modern Portuguese corpus (1998 edition), without stopword removal.

figure.head: TM applying the LDA topic model package to the raw corpus of the 1998 edition with modern Portuguese orthography.
figure.figDesc: The ten highest-probability terms for each of ten topics in the raw 1998 corpus, with Topic 5 dominated by high-frequency function words.

figure.head: Hierarchical clustering of the TM results from analyzing the raw corpus of the 1998 edition with modern Portuguese orthography.
figure.figDesc: Hierarchical clustering of the topics from the raw 1998 corpus, showing Topic 5 as an outlier associated with the absence of stopword removal.

div.p: Figures 5 and 6, which correspond to the raw modernized-Portuguese corpus from the 1998 edition (i.e., without token removal or stopword filtering), show a pattern similar to the 1982 corpus under comparable preprocessing conditions. High-frequency function words such as que (that), de (of), and a (the) receive substantial probability mass in at least one topic and therefore stand out relative to other topics. The hierarchical clustering (used here as an exploratory visualization of similarity among topic-word distributions) likewise highlights this effect: One topic (Topic 5) is dominated by grammatical stopwords and appears as an outlier. We interpret this as a stopword topic that primarily captures high-frequency, weakly informative lexical material, illustrating how limited preprocessing can reduce interpretability and distort downstream summaries.

Although the 1982 and 1998 editions differ in the ordering of fragments, our topic model results are broadly similar. This should not be taken as evidence that the model captures narrative ordering or an internal logic of the work: The LDA approach used here is a bag-of-words model and is therefore insensitive to document order (and to word order within fragments). The similarity is thus consistent with the model’s order-invariance and reflects similarity in overall lexical co-occurrence patterns across the corpora.

div.head: Condition 4
div.p: In Condition 4, the unsupervised LDA topic model algorithm was applied to a cleaned modern Portuguese corpus (1998 edition), with stopword removal.

figure.head: TM applying the LDA topic model package to the cleaned corpus of the 1998 edition with modern Portuguese orthography.
figure.figDesc: The ten highest-probability terms for each of ten topics in the cleaned 1998 corpus, including an existential lexical grouping in Topic 8 centred on life, being, soul, nothingness, and dreams.

figure.head: Hierarchical clustering of the TM results from analyzing the cleaned corpus of the 1998 edition with modern Portuguese orthography.
figure.figDesc: Hierarchical clustering of the topics from the cleaned 1998 corpus, showing Topic 8 as comparatively distinct from the remaining topic groupings.

div.p: Condition 4 also yields results similar to those of the 1982 edition. The four analyses highlight the critical importance of data cleaning and demonstrate how corpus preparation influences the outcomes of computational analysis. Topic 8, from the TM model presented in Figure 7, is characterized by abstract and general terms, including vida (life), ser (to be), mim (me), alma (soul), nada (nothing), nunca (never), ter (to have), coisa (thing), coisas (things), and sonho (dream). This topic exhibits a notable prominence across the entire corpus, distinguishing it from the other topics.

As in the previous analysis, the results of the topic modeling are similar across the two editions — 1982 and 1998. Choosing one corpus over the other should depend on the nature of the study. The modern Portuguese edition has the advantage of not requiring the manual addition of archaic Portuguese stopwords to the default list, which may reduce the time and effort needed to prepare and analyse the corpus. On the other hand, from a linguistic perspective, some studies may wish to compare orthographies from different historical periods or prefer to examine the orthography used by the author himself.

From the perspective of Pessoa studies, as mentioned earlier, it is notable that the analyses of both corpora yield similar results, despite the fact that the editions differ significantly in the ordering of the fragments and in their interpretative framing of Pessoa’s aesthetics, according to specialist editors. This suggests that some recurrent lexical configurations remain visible across different editorial presentations of The Book of Disquiet, which is expected — of course — given the model’s indifference to structure. It does not demonstrate, though, that readers interpret the editions in the same way, nor that editorial sequencing has no literary effect. Rather, it indicates the limits of topic modeling for addressing questions of sequence, narrative arrangement, and readerly experience, and suggests that such questions require complementary methods, including close reading and attention to the editorial history of the work.

div.head: 3.2. Comparison between unsupervised LDA and guided seededlda
div.p: While corpus preparation is crucial, the computational method used for analysis is equally important. We model topics with unsupervised LDA using seededlda::textmodel_lda(), applied to the quanteda document-feature matrix (dfm), constructed from the LdoD corpus. The model is data-driven and therefore appropriate for exploratory analysis, but the topics it produces may not align with specific interpretive frameworks or research objectives. The quality of the results depends heavily on the processing of text data, as evidenced in our prior analyses in Section 3.1. In contrast, the guided seededlda package employs a seeded LDA approach through the textmodel_seededlda function, led by a predefined dictionary of seed words (seed_dict). This dictionary anchors the model by associating specific terms with each of the 10 topics. By incorporating prior knowledge or interpretative frameworks, this method ensures that the discovered topics are more closely aligned with theoretical constructs or research goals. However, its effectiveness depends on the seed dictionary: Overly restrictive seed words may limit the model’s ability to detect emergent patterns outside the predefined framework.

Because Pessoa scholarship supports multiple interpretive frameworks, we treat seed selection as a deliberate and contestable modeling choice rather than a neutral encoding of meaning. The seed dictionary represents one possible operationalization of concepts that are prominent in critical readings of Livro do Desassossego. We therefore document the selected seed words explicitly and interpret the seeded model as a guided exploratory procedure, not as a definitive thematic classification of the work.

The primary distinction between the two modeling configurations examined here is the degree of guidance introduced into topic formation. In the unsupervised setting, topics emerge from co-occurrence patterns in the data without external constraints, making this configuration well suited for exploratory analysis and hypothesis generation. In the seeded (guided) setting, the model incorporates a researcher-defined dictionary of seed terms, encouraging topics to remain aligned with predefined concepts while still allowing data-driven variation. Whereas unsupervised LDA prioritizes discovery, seeded LDA can explore interpretability by anchoring selected topics to theoretical frames. To compare these two configurations, we established two corresponding analytical conditions:

list.item: Condition 5: unsupervised LDA topic model package applied to a cleaned modern Portuguese corpus from the 1998 edition, with stopword removal.
Condition 6: (seeded/guided): Seeded (guided) LDA package applied to a cleaned modern Portuguese corpus from the 1998 edition, with stopword removal.

div.p: This comparison highlights the different outcomes, aided by the visualizations derived from analyzing the same corpus using different computational methods. The unsupervised LDA topic model analysis captures a more generic existential vocabulary across topics, with frequent terms such as vida (life), alma (soul), ser (to be), and sonho (dream) dominating the results. These common terms underscore certain narrative nodes within Pessoa’s writing. These nodes can be interpreted as themes that are developed throughout the narrative of the work, while still preserving its fragmentary nature. Further studies should compare this topic model with other works by Pessoa’s heteronyms. The heteronyms were fictional authorial identities created by Fernando Pessoa, each with their own distinct biography, literary style, philosophy, and worldview. Unlike mere pseudonyms, Pessoa’s heteronyms functioned as fully developed literary personas — such as Alberto Caeiro, Ricardo Reis, and Álvaro de Campos — who not only wrote in different styles but also commented on each other's works. This complex literary strategy allowed Pessoa to explore multiple facets of thought, emotion, and aesthetics within a single body of authorship, turning his oeuvre into a polyphonic dialogue of selves.

The guided seededlda analysis produces more tailored results due to its reliance on seed words, including Lisboa (Lisbon), viagem (travel), sonho (dream), literatura (literature), escritório (office), desassossego (disquiet), sentir (to feel), pensar (to think), realidade (reality), and escrita (writing). These seeds were selected based on an interpretative understanding of Pessoa’s work, resulting in a model that highlights concrete concepts central to The Book of Disquiet. This tailored approach enables the analysis to focus on terms particularly relevant to Pessoa’s aesthetic themes, such as Lisbon, disquiet, and the nature of reality. Topic 6 continues to be present in any case.

It is essential, however, to acknowledge that the reliability of the guided seededlda output is contingent upon subjective interpretive choices made during the seed-word selection process. Different interpretations or seed word selections could naturally yield varying results. Conversely, the unsupervised LDA topic model outcome, while less tailored, provides a systematic, data-driven approach that can uncover broader patterns in the text. Rather than viewing one output as more reliable than the other, it is beneficial to consider both models as offering complementary insights. The unsupervised LDA topic model approach reveals an unsupervised structure of topics, while the guided seededlda approach emphasizes supervised themes and structures in Pessoa’s work.

The primary distinction between these two approaches lies in their levels of guidance. Unsupervised models, like those generated by the unsupervised LDA topic model, are suitable for discovering unknown patterns in the text, making them valuable for hypothesis generation. Supervised or semi-supervised models, such as those produced by the guided seededlda, enhance interpretability by anchoring topics to predefined theoretical frames. This dual perspective aligns with classical hermeneutics of Pessoa’s work, offering both emergent and guided insights.

How can these analyses be applied to literary studies? An unsupervised model, such as that provided by the unsupervised LDA topic model, can identify topics that might escape traditional interpretations of the work under study. For instance, in this case, it might be valuable to investigate fragments of The Book of Disquiet using keywords from topics that appear unusual or unexpected. On the other hand, a supervised model, such as the guided seededlda, can be used to trace terms in The Book of Disquiet related to the predefined seeds of the initial search. Together, these methods offer complementary approaches for exploring textual patterns: The unsupervised model uncovers emergent themes, while the supervised model aligns findings with specific interpretative frameworks, enriching the study of literary texts like Pessoa’s Book of Disquiet.

Of the TM examples, which best describes Fernando Pessoa's work? To what extent can we consider these calculations valid? The results demonstrate the importance of specifying how to model and prepare the data that will be analyzed. In line with the positions of
We can start by considering what is being referred to in the phrase information visualization and how it contrasts with that of modeling interpretation. The standard approach to information visualization is to generate a graphic from live or static data. The process is relatively straightforward. A set of quantitative values is charted on a grid, plane, or space governed by a regular, standard metric. Columns, bars, pie charts, points, lines, network diagrams, and so on are all produced in this way. The interpretative work of shaping the data disappears from view in the final result. The image displayed on screen, in print, or through other output devices appears as a statement of fact. The interpretative dimensions of the activity that shaped the data are rendered invisible, not so much concealed as simply missing from view, absent without a trace . and , mappings are constructions of meaning. For instance, Andrew Piper’s Enumerations: Data and Literary Study argues for the integration of computational methods into literary studies, emphasizing that data modeling is not merely a tool but an interpretative act. He highlights how the repetitive patterns in literature, often overlooked, are crucial for understanding broader literary trends. Piper critiques binary thinking in the field (such as close vs. distant reading) and advocates for an approach that combines quantitative and qualitative methods. Through computational models, scholars can test their insights across larger corpora, allowing for new forms of generalization and interpretation that deepen traditional literary analysis: Algorithms require that we define every step of our intellectual process. In their simplest sense, they are nothing more than a set of instructions. Humanists have traditionally been opaque about their methods — about what evidence has been considered and what is considered as evidence. Computation, too, is no stranger to opacity. But done well and done openly, mediating knowledge through computational modeling is neither an enclosure of knowledge nor an act of dehumanization. At its best, it can be understood as a practice of mirroring, one where we show ourselves the cognitive steps we are taking to arrive at an argument about literature, what Walter Benjamin might have called an awareness of a text’s lexical unconscious .

Ultimately, Piper asserts that computational models construct meaning in the same way traditional interpretations do, reframing the act of reading as inherently shaped by the tools and assumptions used in analysis. This aligns with the idea that modeling is also an interpretation, where decisions about data building reflect theoretical choices, merging computation with the critical practices of the humanities. Along with Piper, we believe that both the code and the data preparation process should be clearly described alongside the analyses, ensuring that the analysis is replicable under the same terms, and that the steps leading to an argument or model are fully outlined.

The use of topic modeling in digital humanities and social sciences, according to some researchers like Anna Shadrova, fails to capture linguistic and conceptual content due to unclear assumptions, resulting in unverifiable models . Shadrova's critique highlights the inherent limitations of using topic modeling for content analysis in fields that require deep conceptual understanding, such as linguistics and literary studies. Her argument emphasizes the gap between the computational efficiency of topic models and the interpretive depth required in humanistic research. While topic modeling has gained popularity for its ability to process large corpora quickly, Shadrova argues that this speed often comes at the expense of accuracy and depth.

An obvious next step, in this regard, would be to explore potential hybrid approaches that combine the computational power of topic models with more qualitative, human-centered methods (e.g., as in ). Topic modeling could be seen as an invitation to interpretation, rather than a description of facts. When working with such tools and analyses, it is crucial to clarify the processes by which we shape the data. Does it matter that we get different TM results from different tools, or even from the same tool with different data treatments? If we consider the results as facts, this could compromise the accuracy and depth of the analysis. However, if we view the results as constructions and specify how the data was processed, then TM can be understood as a step in the literary interpretation process, with its accuracy depending on the discourse that links TM to literary interpretation.

div.head: 4. Discussion: On the importance of transparency
div.p: This detailed process of preparing and structuring a corpus highlights how many interpretive decisions are made before any modeling even begins. Our comparison of topic models across Pessoa’s editions and corpora construction has shown that such decisions, from cleaning to metadata handling, can shape the output, even if subtly. To ensure these processes are robust and reproducible, we must turn our attention to how transparency in corpus construction and analyses are done.
A corpus is rarely just a collection of raw, unedited texts grouped together. To effectively run a dataset through a corpus analysis program, we normally need to:

list.item: Remove noise or unwanted text, such as headers, footnotes, or irrelevant metadata (after OCR procedures are complete, if applicable);
Divide the corpus into segments (normally tokens, sentences, or larger structural units);
Add layers of annotation (or information) to the text, including tagging parts of speech, named entities, or semantic roles (if applicable); and
Document and store information about the text itself, such as the source, authorship, and publication details.

div.p: These pieces of information should ideally be structured in a way that allows them to be easily retrieved and reused in future research.

Messy or poorly documented data can pose serious challenges to transparency in research. When performing data analysis, a large portion of the time is spent on data cleaning and preparation — some estimates suggest that data tidying consumes around 80% of the data analysis process . This heavy workload can be significantly reduced if the data collection process is executed carefully, with an emphasis on minimizing noise and ensuring clarity. Moreover, proper data collection in the first place allows for the preservation of crucial information about the data, such as the author’s name, date of publication, and source, which may prove vital for future analysis or replication efforts. Metadata of this kind is often key to ensuring transparency, as it allows other researchers to trace the lineage and context of the data.

We suggest that there are three ways of contributing to tidy and well-documented datasets. First, it is essential to always retain the original data in its raw format, as obtained from the source. Preserving the data in its original state ensures that researchers or future users can revisit the initial version for alternative approaches to data cleaning or analysis. This practice provides flexibility and transparency, as any modifications or transformations made to the data are fully traceable. The ability to return to the raw data can also safeguard against biases introduced during cleaning processes, where crucial information could inadvertently be removed.

Second, it is important to retain as much metadata as possible. While certain metadata may seem irrelevant to the immediate research questions, it could be crucial for future projects or different research contexts. For instance, metadata such as the genre of the text, regional or temporal variations, or even the platform from which the text was sourced can significantly impact how the data is interpreted or processed. Ensuring comprehensive metadata documentation also enables future users to reproduce or verify the findings, a key aspect of transparency in research.

Third, researchers must have a clear understanding of how the data is being collected and processed. The research questions should drive the selection of data collection and processing tools — not the other way around. If there is already a piece of software suitable for the task, adopting this tool can drastically reduce the data processing time, if its process is clear (and not a black box) for the investigator. However, very often when collecting specific datasets, developing a customised script might be an easier solution. By doing this, we avoid having many dependencies in our code (i.e., a piece of software that relies on external code packages). And, with our code, we can keep things simple and easily controlled, making customizations and updates more convenient. Choosing the right source format can also increase the quality of the data or reduce the preparation time. Sometimes, the same data content is available in multiple formats (e.g., PDF, HTML, plain text, or XML). While plain text formats are generally easier to work with, they may lack the structural information (such as section breaks, paragraph divisions, or hyperlinks) that other formats, such as XML, can retain. Preserving such structure can enhance analysis, especially when performing discourse analysis or tracking thematic shifts across sections. A good practice is to experiment with different data formats or sources to assess which is best suited to the research project at hand.

While the processes outlined above contribute to more transparent research practices, it is crucial to strike a balance between efficiency and thoroughness. Striving for transparency does not necessarily mean sacrificing time or effort; rather, it means approaching the data preparation process with a mindset of clarity, documentation, and traceability. By preserving original data, retaining rich metadata, understanding data collection methods, and choosing appropriate data formats, researchers can build corpora that are not only optimized for analysis but also transparent and reusable for future studies.

We can summarize the guide for using topic modeling in digital humanities as follows: (a) Data cleaning, (b) Data preservation, (c) Data management, and (d) Data interpretation. Keeping records of all data preparation steps is necessary for transparency and future reproducibility. Efficient workflows in literary studies often depend on balancing the advantages of computational tools with the interpretive depth required by the discipline. While automation through data selection, cleaning, and topic modeling is essential for handling large corpora, interpretation remains a deeply human task. Computational tools can accelerate discovery, but the role of the digital humanities scholar is to contextualize these discoveries within a framework of historical, thematic, and theoretical concerns. The workflow thus involves a cyclical process: selecting a corpus aligned with the research questions, applying computational tools to uncover hidden structures, describing the tools as theoretical choices, and then interpreting those results to enrich our understanding of literature.

div.head: 5. Conclusion
div.p: The examples above demonstrated only a few of the many parameters that can be altered. We believe that TM is not only a means to identify topics in a dataset, but a tool to help navigate the data, and, as such, it should be used for exploratory data analysis and visualisations. We also believe that making available the commented codes used for the data analysis can be the beginning of more robust documentation codes in digital humanities and allow researchers to discuss and build on existing practices in TM.

There is, however, a range of fundamental issues with topic modeling itself that need to be considered. First, the topic modeling algorithm is stochastic, and as such, there may be slight variations in the output each time it is run. Not only does this have implications for replicability, but it also has implications for the study discussed in the present paper. In effect, how do we know which of the differences between our four conditions were the result of parameter manipulation, and which were the result of random variation inherent in the TM process? Ultimately, when digital humanities scholars carry out their own analyses, we would recommend either running the algorithm a single time and using that as their output (as we did here); or running it multiple times, noting variation between topics, and then giving higher interpretive prominence to those terms that are stable across multiple runs.

Second, there is a potential problem in the terminology being used. The word topic takes on two meanings within the topic modeling literature, and neither of them refers to the third traditional definition as understood by social scientists (i.e., a central matter being discussed in the text). The first meaning is the list of words derived by the algorithm — essentially, the group of words that satisfy the model according to certain probabilistic patterns . The second meaning is the topic label that is imposed on the list of words by the researcher. Indeed, neither of these can accurately be claimed to represent the text without further exploration. There is a missing validity check to ensure that these meanings are consistent.

Third, intuitive interpretations based on superficial scrutiny of the top 10 words are easy to come up with, but this is often incomplete or incorrect upon detailed examination of discourse and eyeballing is not enough . And fourth, this interpretation may change depending on the analyst’s specialist knowledge (or lack thereof), and it also differs depending on differences in perspective, or how the subject is construed. These slight variations in construal are not likely to be captured by a topic model, even though such nuanced differences are of interest for literary analysis.

Does this mean that TM is unsuitable for literary or linguistic analysis? We argue that when research emphasizes transparency, TM can serve as an initial step toward interpretation, especially within corpus analysis. Rather than merely describing facts, TM offers a reading that is shaped by frequency patterns. The examples we observed with the different topic models applied to Pessoa's work highlight how the algorithm, along with decisions regarding the corpus, shape the data. This process of shaping is an act of representation, and as such, it carries an epistemological dimension that must be acknowledged. Computational analyses are not mere facts; they are forms of representation, with all the philosophical implications that this entails.

A lack of transparency — specifically, not knowing the methods and data used for the analysis — can negatively impact the results. Decisions that may seem relatively innocuous at first (e.g., choosing to tag data, accepting grammatical categorization as valid, stopword removal, etc.) are still theoretical decisions and should be documented like any other methodological choice, including the tools used for the analyses. We believe that providing clear documentation and explanations of all the steps taken in textual data analysis can improve understanding and lead to better outcomes when replicating computational methods applied to language and literary studies.

div.head: Data and Materials
div.p: All supplementary materials created for this article are openly accessible on Zenodo: http://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21201714. The repository includes the R Markdown workflows, metadata, custom stopword lists, R session information, derived token files, chunked and shuffled token files, and topic-term outputs generated by the workflows. For reproducibility, the repository separates the preprocessing and modeling stages. The PDF-based R Markdown file documents how the public shuffled-token CSV files were generated from local source files and is provided for methodological transparency. The main reproducibility file starts from the deposited CSV files and allows readers to rerun the topic modeling experiments without access to the original PDFs.
